lead: Both readings are about words. In Isaiah, God’s word goes out like rain and does not come back empty. In Matthew, Jesus warns against the piling up of words and gives us a few that are enough. God’s word comes down to us, does its work, and returns; the Our Father is the word that carries us back to him. The key words are word, Father and forgive.

r.h: My word shall not return to me empty
set: Isaiah 40–55, the Book of Consolation, speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Many scholars think it comes from an unnamed prophet of the exile, in the tradition of Isaiah. Chapter 55 is its closing invitation, opening with “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters” (55:1).

The exiles had reason to doubt. Jerusalem lay in ruins, and God’s promises looked like words that had come to nothing. Just before our reading God says that his ways and thoughts are as high above ours as the heavens are above the earth (55:9). These two verses then show that what is high does not stay high: it comes down.
str: v. 10: the picture: rain and snow come down, water the earth, and give seed and bread.
v. 11: the comparison: so shall my word be.
¶ It is one long sentence in Hebrew, built on “as” and “so”.
kw: In Hebrew this means both a word and a thing done. God’s word is not a sound that fades. It acts: “God said” and it was so (Genesis 1).
Empty-handed, with nothing to show. It is the word for someone who comes back from a journey having gained nothing.
To bring something to a good end. The word itself, sent out on an errand like a messenger, finishes the task it was given.
vv: For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there until they have watered the earth,
The prophet is careful with the order: the rain goes back up only after the ground has drunk. Growth is slow and hidden, and the farmer does not see it happen.
giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater,
The gift is double: bread for today, seed for next year.
so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose,
The promise does not say that we will always see the result, or see it soon. It says that the word will do what God intends.
ch: Christians hear in this picture the whole path of Jesus, the Word made flesh. He says, “I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father” (John 16:28). The Second Vatican Council speaks of the great force and power in the word of God, the support and energy of the Church (Dei Verbum 21; CCC 131). For those who preach and teach, and for parents who repeat the faith to children who seem not to listen, this is a verse of real comfort.

set: We are in the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has just spoken about three practices of Jewish piety: almsgiving, prayer and fasting (6:1–18), the same three the Church takes up in Lent. In each he says: do it for the Father, who sees in secret. At the centre of that teaching he sets the Our Father.

Luke has a shorter form of the prayer (Luke 11:2–4), and Matthew’s longer form is the one the Church prays. Matthew’s setting is a teaching on how to pray; Luke’s is the disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us to pray”.
str: vv. 7–8: not many words: the Father already knows.
vv. 9–10: three petitions for God: his name, his kingdom, his will.
vv. 11–13: our needs: bread, forgiveness, protection.
vv. 14–15: a comment on one petition alone: forgiveness.
kw: The word is rare and its exact meaning is uncertain; it may imitate the sound of babbling. The warning is against the idea that a great many words can wear God down.

Found almost nowhere outside this prayer, so its sense is debated: for today, for tomorrow, or what we need to live. The Catechism gathers the meanings: our needs for this day, and also, taken literally as “super-essential”, the Bread of Life, the Body of Christ (CCC 2837).
Matthew’s word is “debts”, Luke’s is “sins”. In the Aramaic of that time the word for a debt was also used for sin. We stand before God as people who owe what they cannot pay.
vv: for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Then why ask? Not to inform God, but because prayer changes the one who prays: it makes us children who trust.
Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.
“Our”, not “my”: no one prays this prayer alone. “Hallowed be” asks God himself to make his name known as holy (compare Ezekiel 36:23; CCC 2807–2808).
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

This is the one petition with a condition in it, and the only one Jesus goes back to explain (vv. 14–15). The Catechism says that God’s mercy cannot penetrate a heart that refuses to forgive (CCC 2840).
And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.

A note on the text. The closing words “For the kingdom and the power and the glory are yours” are not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew and are not printed in the NRSV’s main text or in the POC. A form of them appears in the very old Didache, and the Roman Mass says similar words after the prayer that follows the Our Father. “The evil one” is a person, Satan, not an abstraction (CCC 2851).
ch: Tertullian called the Lord’s Prayer “truly the summary of the whole gospel”, and St Thomas Aquinas called it the most perfect of prayers (CCC 2761, 2763). The closing section of the Catechism is a commentary on it, petition by petition (CCC 2759–2865). The Church prays it at every Mass as the family’s preparation for Communion.

qa: If Jesus warned against many words, why do Catholics say the Rosary or a litany?

The warning is against the belief that the amount of words will force God’s hand. Jesus himself in Gethsemane “prayed for the third time, saying the same words” (Matthew 26:44). The Catechism says that the repeated invocation of a holy name is not heaping up empty phrases, but a holding fast to the word (CCC 2668). Repetition said with love is like a child who says the same thing to a mother many times.
study: Where have I seen God’s word working slowly, long after it was first spoken to me?
Which line of the Our Father is hardest for me to say honestly today? Whom do I need to forgive so that I can say it?
